\begin{proof}
\medskip\noindent\emph{Imported source scope.}
In \cite[Example~6.7.2]{CLD25}, Chambert--Loir and Ducros put a
\(G\)-tropical affine structure on an interval
\(I\subseteq\overline{\mathbf R}\), with
\(A=\partial I\cap\overline{\mathbf R}\), by requiring parlinear functions
to be constant near every point of \(A\).  In particular, every affine
function on a connected domain meeting \(A\) is constant.  Fix a finite
endpoint \(a\in A\cap\mathbf R\).  Together with their definition of smooth
forms in \cite[Definition~6.2.1]{CLD25}, the example says the following.
By \cite[\S\S6.1.1 and 6.1.6]{CLD25}, a tropical chart is affine and each of
its scalar coordinate functions is affine.  After shrinking to a connected
neighbourhood meeting \(A\), Example~6.7.2 therefore makes every coordinate
constant.  The chart, and every smooth \(0\)-form pulled back through it, is
constant there.  Use the ordinary inward real coordinate on the finite
stratum and extend it topologically by the value \(t(a)=0\); this is not a
nonconstant affine chart through \(a\).  In this coordinate, the smooth
functions are precisely the functions described by
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-collar-smoothness}.  Conversely, use the constant
terminal chart on the collar and the ordinary coordinate \(t\) on
endpoint-free interior neighbourhoods; these local descriptions glue.  On
the one-dimensional interior,
\[
 \mathrm d'\mathrm d'' f
   =f''(t)\,\mathrm d't\wedge\mathrm d''t,
\]
so positivity is exactly \eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-stage-zero}; the form
vanishes on the collar where \(f\) is constant.  Definition~8.1.1 and
Lemma~8.1.4 of \cite{CLD25} give the generated sheaf and its ordinal
filtration used in the statement.  We will also use the elementary
uniform-to-monotone device of \cite[Lemma~8.1.10]{CLD25}: if real-valued
functions \(f_j\) converge uniformly to \(f\) on a set \(K\), then
\[
                  f_j+2\lVert f_j-f\rVert_{K}
\]
has a decreasing subsequence converging uniformly to \(f\).

\medskip\noindent\emph{The comparison class is a sheaf.}
Restrictions in \(\mathscr J_{\partial}\) are immediate.  We check
gluing.  Suppose that \(W=\bigcup_{\nu}W_\nu\) and that
\(u|_{W_\nu}\in\mathscr J_{\partial}(W_\nu)\) for every \(\nu\).  Let
\(C\) be a connected component of \(W\).  The function \(u|_C\) is locally
extended-real convex.

We first show that \(u|_C\) is either finite everywhere or identically
\(-\infty\).  Let
\[
 Z=\{t\in C:u(t)=-\infty\},
 \qquad
 F=C\setminus Z.
\]
If \(t\in Z\) is an interior point of \(C\), choose an interval
\((t-\delta,t+\delta)\cap C\) on which \(u\) is convex.  For a point
\(s>t\) sufficiently close to \(t\), choose \(q>s\) in that interval and
write \(s\) as a strict convex combination of \(t\) and \(q\).
Then \eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-extended-convexity} gives \(u(s)=-\infty\).
The same argument on the left shows that \(Z\) is open at \(t\).  If
\(0\in Z\), choose \(a>0\) such that \(u\) is convex on \([0,a)\).
For \(0<s<a\), choose \(q\in(s,a)\) and write
\(s=(1-s/q)0+(s/q)q\); again \(u(s)=-\infty\).  Thus \(Z\) is open also
at the endpoint.

If \(t\in F\) is an interior point and there were points \(s\in Z\)
arbitrarily close to \(t\), choose such an \(s\) and a point \(q\) on the
other side of \(t\), all in one interval of local convexity.  Expressing
\(t\) as a strict convex combination of \(s\) and \(q\) would give
\(u(t)=-\infty\), a contradiction.  Hence \(F\) is open at every interior
point.  If \(0\in F\), the local instance of
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-boundary-minimum} excludes the value
\(-\infty\) on a whole initial interval, so \(F\) is open at \(0\) as
well.  Since \(C\) is connected, either \(Z=C\) or \(F=C\).

In the finite case, the standard one-dimensional local-to-global
criterion shows that \(u|_C\) is convex.  Here is a direct verification.
Given \(a<c<b\) in \(C\), cover \([a,b]\) by finitely many intervals on
which \(u\) is convex.  Take a Lebesgue number \(\delta>0\) for this finite
cover of \([a,b]\), and choose a partition
\[
             a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=b
\]
that contains \(c\) and satisfies
\(x_{i+1}-x_{i-1}<\delta\) whenever the three terms occur.  Each interval
\([x_{i-1},x_{i+1}]\) then lies in one member of the cover.  Local convexity
therefore says that the successive secant slopes are nondecreasing.  Summing
the resulting inequalities on the two sides of \(c\) yields
\[
 \frac{u(c)-u(a)}{c-a}
 \leq
 \frac{u(b)-u(c)}{b-c},
\]
which is equivalent to the convexity inequality at \(c\).  Thus
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-extended-convexity} holds on every interval in
\(C\).  It is automatic when \(u|_C\equiv-\infty\).

It remains to propagate the boundary minimum.  Suppose \(0\in C\), fix
\(t\in C\), and choose \(s\in(0,1)\) so small that \(st\) lies with \(0\)
in one member of the cover.  There
\[
                              u(0)\leq u(st).
\]
If \(u(0)=-\infty\), the desired inequality is automatic.  If
\(u(0)\in\mathbf R\), the preceding dichotomy makes \(u\) finite on
\(C\), while global convexity gives
\[
                 u(st)\leq(1-s)u(0)+s u(t).
\]
Combining the last two inequalities, cancelling \((1-s)u(0)\), and
dividing by \(s\) gives \(u(0)\leq u(t)\).  This proves the gluing axiom
and hence that \(\mathscr J_{\partial}\) is a sheaf.

\medskip\noindent\emph{The generated sheaf is contained in the comparison
class.}
The sheaf \(\mathscr J_{\partial}\) is stable under pointwise decreasing
limits.  Indeed, every inequality
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-extended-convexity} passes to the limit in
\(\mathbf R\cup\{-\infty\}\), since no \(+\infty\) value occurs, and
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-boundary-minimum} passes to the limit as well.

It also contains \(\operatorname{Psh}_{S,0}\).  On an interior interval,
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-stage-zero} gives ordinary convexity.  On the
component meeting \(0\), the derivative of a generator is zero on the
constant collar and is nondecreasing thereafter; consequently the
generator is convex on the whole half-interval and takes its minimum at
\(0\).  By the minimal definition of the generated psh sheaf,
\begin{equation}
                       \operatorname{Psh}_S
                       \subseteq\mathscr J_{\partial}.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-generated-in-jensen}
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent\emph{The extended-real alternatives at the endpoint.}
Let \(0\in W\) and \(u\in\mathscr J_{\partial}(W)\).  After shrinking its
connected component, choose \(R>0\) with \([0,R)\subseteq W\).

Suppose first that \(u(0)=-\infty\).  For \(0<t<R\), choose
\(q\in(t,R)\).  Since
\[
                         t=(1-t/q)0+(t/q)q,
\]
extended-real convexity gives
\[
 u(t)\leq(1-t/q)u(0)+(t/q)u(q)=-\infty.
\]
Thus \(u\equiv-\infty\) on \([0,R)\).  The smooth psh constants \(-n\)
decrease to this function on the fixed neighbourhood.

Assume now that
\begin{equation}
                              u(0)\in\mathbf R.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-finite-value}
\end{equation}
The boundary minimum excludes \(-\infty\) at every other point, so \(u\)
is real-valued.  For \(0<s<t<R\), convexity and
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-boundary-minimum} give
\begin{equation}
 u(s)
 \leq\left(1-\frac{s}{t}\right)u(0)+\frac{s}{t}u(t)
 \leq u(t).
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-monotonicity}
\end{equation}
Hence \(u\) is nondecreasing.  It is continuous in the interior by
ordinary finite convexity.  At the endpoint, for any fixed \(t\in(0,R)\),
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-boundary-minimum} and the first inequality in
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-monotonicity} show that
\[
 u(0)\leq u(s)
 \leq u(0)+\frac{s}{t}\bigl(u(t)-u(0)\bigr)
 \quad(0<s<t),
\]
so \(u(s)\to u(0)\) as \(s\downarrow0\).  Thus \(u\) is continuous on
\([0,R)\).

\medskip\noindent\emph{A fixed-domain collar regularization.}
Choose
\[
                         0<r<R_1<R_2<R.
\]
Put
\[
                         m=
             \frac{u(R_2)-u(R_1)}{R_2-R_1}\geq0
\]
and define a finite function \(\bar u:\mathbf R\to\mathbf R\) by
\begin{equation}
 \bar u(t)=
 \begin{cases}
  u(0),&t\leq0,\\
  u(t),&0\leq t\leq R_1,\\
  u(R_1)+m(t-R_1),&t\geq R_1.
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-convex-extension}
\end{equation}
This extension is convex and nondecreasing.  At \(0\), the left slope is
zero and every right secant slope is nonnegative by
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-boundary-minimum}.  At \(R_1\), convexity of
\(u\) shows that every left secant slope is at most the secant slope
\(m\) to \(R_2\).  The one-dimensional slope criterion for convexity
therefore applies at both joining points.

Fix a nonnegative even function
\(\theta\in C^\infty_c((-1,1))\) with integral one, and put
\(\theta_\sigma(s)=\sigma^{-1}\theta(s/\sigma)\).  For a sequence
\(\sigma_j\downarrow0\), define
\begin{equation}
                         A_j=\bar u*\theta_{\sigma_j}.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-convolution}
\end{equation}
Every \(A_j\) is smooth, convex, and nondecreasing.  Evenness gives
\(\int s\theta_{\sigma_j}(s)\,\mathrm ds=0\), so Jensen's inequality
gives
\begin{equation}
                              A_j\geq\bar u.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-convolution-dominates}
\end{equation}
Moreover, \(A_j\to\bar u\) uniformly on every compact interval.

We next impose exact constancy on a collar.  For \(\eta>0\), set
\begin{equation}
 M_\eta(a,b)=
 \int_{\mathbf R^2}
 \max\{a+s_1,b+s_2\}
 \theta_\eta(s_1)\theta_\eta(s_2)\,
 \mathrm ds_1\,\mathrm ds_2.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-regularized-maximum}
\end{equation}
This function is smooth, convex, and nondecreasing in each variable.
The zero first moments and the support of the kernel give
\begin{equation}
 \max\{a,b\}
 \leq M_\eta(a,b)
 \leq\max\{a,b\}+\eta.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-regularized-max-bounds}
\end{equation}
If \(a>b+2\eta\), then \(a+s_1>b+s_2\) throughout the convolution
support and \(M_\eta(a,b)=a\); symmetrically,
\begin{equation}
 M_\eta(a,b)=b
 \quad\text{whenever}\quad b>a+2\eta.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-regularized-max-truncation}
\end{equation}

Choose \(\varepsilon_j\downarrow0\), put
\(\eta_j=\varepsilon_j/4\), and define
\begin{equation}
 H_j(t)=M_{\eta_j}(t,\varepsilon_j),
 \qquad
 F_j(t)=A_j\bigl(H_j(t)\bigr).
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-collar-approximants}
\end{equation}
The function \(H_j\) is smooth, convex, and nondecreasing.  From
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-regularized-max-bounds} one gets, for \(t\geq0\),
\begin{equation}
 0\leq H_j(t)-t\leq\varepsilon_j+\eta_j.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-reparametrization-error}
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-regularized-max-truncation},
\begin{equation}
 H_j(t)=\varepsilon_j
 \quad\text{for}\quad
 0\leq t<\varepsilon_j-2\eta_j
                =\frac{\varepsilon_j}{2}.
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-exact-collar}
\end{equation}
Consequently \(F_j\) is smooth and exactly constant on an initial
interval.

The function \(F_j\) is convex.  Indeed, \(A_j'\geq0\),
\(A_j''\geq0\), \(H_j'\geq0\), and \(H_j''\geq0\), so
\[
 F_j''
  =A_j''(H_j)(H_j')^2+A_j'(H_j)H_j''
  \geq0.
\]
Thus \(F_j|_{[0,r)}\) belongs to
\(\operatorname{Psh}_{S,0}([0,r))\).  It also dominates \(u\) on
\([0,r]\): by monotonicity of \(A_j\),
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-reparametrization-error}, and
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-convolution-dominates},
\begin{equation}
 F_j(t)=A_j(H_j(t))
 \geq A_j(t)
 \geq\bar u(t)=u(t).
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-smooth-domination}
\end{equation}

Finally, \(F_j\to u\) uniformly on \(K=[0,r]\).  For all sufficiently
large \(j\), both \(t\) and \(H_j(t)\) lie in the fixed compact interval
\([0,r+1]\).  Hence
\begin{align}
 \sup_{t\in K}|F_j(t)-u(t)|
 &\leq
 \sup_{x\in[0,r+1]}|A_j(x)-\bar u(x)|
 \notag\\
 &\quad+
 \sup_{t\in K}|\bar u(H_j(t))-\bar u(t)|
 \longrightarrow0,
 \label{eq:p071-endpoint-uniform-convergence}
\end{align}
where the second term tends to zero by uniform continuity of \(\bar u\)
and \eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-reparametrization-error}.

Let
\[
                       e_j=\lVert F_j-u\rVert_K.
\]
By \cite[Lemma~8.1.10]{CLD25}, the sequence \(F_j+2e_j\) has a
subsequence, say
\[
                         G_n=F_{j_n}+2e_{j_n},
\]
which decreases uniformly to \(u\) on \(K\).  Adding a constant preserves
smoothness, collar constancy, and convexity.  Restricting to the one fixed
open neighbourhood \(V=[0,r)\) proves
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-fixed-domain-approximation} in the finite case.

\medskip\noindent\emph{Interior points and conclusion.}
Let \(x\in W\cap(0,R_0)\).  On a sufficiently small connected interval
about \(x\), the dichotomy proved above says that a section of
\(\mathscr J_{\partial}\) is either identically \(-\infty\) or is a
finite convex function.  The first case is the decreasing limit of the
smooth psh constants \(-n\).  In the second case, choose a compact
interval \(K=[a,b]\) around \(x\), contained in a slightly larger interval
on which \(u\) is finite and convex.  The one-sided derivatives of a finite
convex function are finite at the interior points \(a,b\).  Choose
\[
                    p_-\in\partial u(a),
                    \qquad p_+\in\partial u(b),
\]
and extend \(u|_{[a,b]}\) by
\[
 u(a)+p_-(t-a)\quad(t<a),
 \qquad
 u(b)+p_+(t-b)\quad(t>b).
\]
Monotonicity of the subgradients makes this a finite convex function on
\(\mathbf R\).  Convolution with the even kernels used in
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-convolution} gives smooth convex functions
converging uniformly to \(u\) on \(K\).  Applying
\cite[Lemma~8.1.10]{CLD25} and restricting to the interior of \(K\)
produces a decreasing sequence of smooth convex functions on one fixed
neighbourhood of \(x\).

We have proved
\[
                 \mathscr J_{\partial}
                 \subseteq\operatorname{Psh}_{S,1}.
\]
The tautological inclusion
\(\operatorname{Psh}_{S,1}\subseteq\operatorname{Psh}_S\), together with
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-generated-in-jensen}, proves
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-first-stage-collapse}.  The construction at the
endpoint gives every assertion following
\eqref{eq:p071-endpoint-fixed-domain-approximation}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Write $c(y)=u(\eta,y)$ near the node.  We use the comparison theorem
\Cref{thm:p071-infinite-star-collapse-candidate}, including its endpoint
trace, slope budget, finite-activity truncation, and finite harmonic
smoothing.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Locality and decreasing closure of the comparison conditions.}
The definition of $\mathcal J_X$ is local, so restriction and gluing are
immediate once the product junction inequality is known to be local.  To
check this point, contract every point occurring in
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-jensen} by a common factor
$0<s<1$ towards $(\eta,y_0)$:
\[
 (-r_i,y_i)\longmapsto
 (-sr_i,\,y_0+s(y_i-y_0)).
\]
The barycentre relation is preserved, with every reciprocal weight
multiplied by $s^{-1}$.  For sufficiently small $s$, all contracted
points lie in one comparison chart at $(\eta,y_0)$.  Write the exceptional
set of that restricted chart as $A\cup E$, enlarging $E\subset B\setminus
A$ harmlessly if necessary.  Retain the contracted data on every original
tuple branch in $A\cup F$.  For each newly exceptional branch
$e\in E\setminus F$, choose any $0<\sigma_e$ in its restricted collar
and add the sample $(-\sigma_e,y_0)$.  The enlarged barycentre relation
still holds, because the new point and the centre have the same Euclidean
coordinate.  With
\[
                  \Theta=\sum_{e\in E\setminus F}\frac1{\sigma_e},
\]
the restricted-chart inequality is
\begin{align*}
 (s^{-1}\Lambda+\Theta)c(y_0)
 &\leq \sum_{b\in F}
   \frac{u_b(-sr_b,y_0+s(y_b-y_0))}{sr_b}\\
 &\quad+\sum_{a\in A}
   \frac{u_a(-s\rho_a,y_0+s(y_a-y_0))}{s\rho_a}
   +\sum_{e\in E\setminus F}
   \frac{u_e(-\sigma_e,y_0)}{\sigma_e}.
\end{align*}
Each newly exceptional branch was full before restriction, so its last
sample is at most $c(y_0)$.  Joint convexity on each original segment gives
\[
 u_i(-sr_i,y_0+s(y_i-y_0))
 \leq (1-s)c(y_0)+s u_i(-r_i,y_i).
\]
Substitution bounds the right side of the restricted-chart inequality by
\[
 (s^{-1}-1)\Lambda c(y_0)
 +\sum_{b\in F}\frac{u_b(-r_b,y_b)}{r_b}
 +\sum_{a\in A}\frac{u_a(-\rho_a,y_a)}{\rho_a}
 +\Theta c(y_0).
\]
Cancelling the two added central contributions proves the original
inequality.  The same argument proves compatibility when a full branch
becomes exceptional after restriction.  Thus the displayed conditions do
define a sheaf.

We next prove sequential closure.  Let $u_n\downarrow u$ on an open set
and fix a node point.  Choose a standard product
$U_0\times V_0$ in that open set and a compact convex set
$Q\Subset V_0$ whose interior contains the Euclidean coordinate of the
point.  For fixed $n$, compactness of $\{\eta\}\times Q$ supplies
finitely many comparison charts for $u_n$.  The union of their finite
exceptional sets and countable activity sets is countable; call it
$K_n$.  Local joint convexity and the contraction argument above extend
the branch and junction conditions across $U_0\times\operatorname{int}Q$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 u_n(p_b(t),y)=u_n(\eta,y)
 \quad
 \bigl(b\notin A\cup K_n,\ t\in[-\infty,0],\ y\in Q\bigr),
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-limit-inactive}
\end{equation}
where $A$ is the finite exceptional set of $U_0$.  Hence the limit has
one countable activity set $\bigcup_nK_n$.

Joint extended-real convexity passes to a decreasing limit.  For each fixed
$y$, the endpoint trace passes by the argument in the exact-star theorem:
monotonicity gives one inequality, and a sufficiently advanced row gives
the reverse inequality, also when the limiting endpoint value is
$-\infty$.  The same specialization, with every Euclidean sample equal
to $y$, shows that each fibre is a member of $\mathscr J_B$.
Suppose now that $c(y_0)$ is finite in a prescribed product junction
tuple.  The scalar exact-star argument shows that every finite-stratum
value in that tuple is finite.  Consequently all terms in the junction
inequality for $u_n$ converge in $\mathbf R$, and termwise passage to
the limit proves \eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-jensen} for $u$.
Thus $\mathcal J_X$ is closed under pointwise decreasing sequential
limits.

Every generator belongs to $\mathcal J_X$.  Only the product junction
condition requires proof.  Put
$d_i=\partial_tg_i(0,y_0)$.  Joint convexity and smoothness give
\[
 g_i(-r_i,y_i)\geq
 c_g(y_0)-r_id_i+
 \nabla c_g(y_0)\mathbin\cdot(y_i-y_0),
\]
where $r_i$ denotes $r_b$ or $\rho_a$.  Divide by $r_i$ and sum
over the selected full branches and all exceptional branches.  The
Euclidean linear terms cancel by
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-barycentre}.  Every omitted full-branch
derivative is nonnegative, since that branch is convex and constant near
$-\infty$.  The balance law
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-smooth-balance} therefore says that the
sum of the selected derivatives is nonpositive.  The remaining inequality
is exactly \eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-jensen}.  Minimality now gives
\begin{equation}
                         \mathcal P_X\subseteq\mathcal J_X.
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-minimality}
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Partial Legendre reduction at a finite node value.}
Let $u\in\mathcal J_X$ near $(\eta,y_0)$, and first suppose that
$c(y_0)\in\mathbf R$.  After shrinking the Euclidean ball, $c$ is
finite: an extended-real convex function on an open convex set cannot take
both a finite value and the value $-\infty$.  Specializing the product
junction condition to equal Euclidean coordinates places every fibre in
$\mathscr J_B$.  The finite-centre part of the exact-star theorem then
shows that all finite-stratum branch values are real.

Use a comparison chart on $U\times V_0$, with exceptional set $A$ and
countable activity set $K$.  Shrink the exceptional collars once.  Let
$D\subset U$ be the resulting compact closed standard core.  Choose an
open convex set $V\ni y_0$ and a compact convex set $Q$ such that
\[
                  \overline V\subset\operatorname{int}Q,
                  \qquad Q\Subset V_0.
\]
For
$p\in(\mathbf R^d)^*$, define
\begin{align}
 f_0(p)&=\min_{y\in Q}\bigl(c(y)-p\mathbin\cdot y\bigr),
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-legendre-centre}\\
 f_b(t,p)&=\min_{y\in Q}
       \bigl(u_b(t,y)-p\mathbin\cdot y\bigr).
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-legendre-branch}
\end{align}
At a full endpoint the second minimum is interpreted in the extended
order.  Its endpoint slice is either finite on the interior of $Q$ or
identically $-\infty$; these are the only possibilities for an
extended-real convex function on a connected open convex set.

For every fixed $p$, the functions in
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-legendre-centre}--%
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-legendre-branch} form a member
$f(\,cdot\,,p)\in\mathscr J_B(D)$.  Convexity in the branch variable
follows by taking minimizing Euclidean points at two branch parameters and
using their convex combination in $Q$.  For a full branch, exact endpoint
trace passes through the minimum: the lower bound follows from
monotonicity, while evaluation at a minimizing endpoint point gives the
upper bound; if the endpoint slice is $-\infty$, evaluation at any fixed
Euclidean point gives convergence to $-\infty$.

It remains to check the finite-point balance.  Choose minimizing points
$y_i\in Q$ for all finitely many branch terms and set
\[
 y_*=\Lambda^{-1}
 \left(\sum_{b\in F}\frac{y_b}{r_b}
       +\sum_{a\in A}\frac{y_a}{\rho_a}\right)\in Q.
\]
Then the product junction inequality gives
\begin{align*}
 \Lambda f_0(p)
 &\leq \Lambda\bigl(c(y_*)-p\mathbin\cdot y_*\bigr)\\
 &\leq
 \sum_{b\in F}\frac{f_b(-r_b,p)}{r_b}
 +\sum_{a\in A}\frac{f_a(-\rho_a,p)}{\rho_a}.
\end{align*}
This is the Jensen form of the scalar exact-star balance.  Finally,
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-countable-activity} gives
\begin{equation}
 f_b(t,p)=f_0(p)
 \quad(b\in B\setminus(A\cup K)).
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-legendre-inactive}
\end{equation}

Conversely, suppose that scalar profiles $h_b(t,p)$ belong to
$\mathscr J_B(D)$ for every $p$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 H_b(t,y)=\sup_p\bigl(p\mathbin\cdot y+h_b(t,p)\bigr)
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-reconstruction}
\end{equation}
is jointly convex on every branch and satisfies the product junction
condition.  Indeed, multiply the scalar Jensen inequality by the
reciprocal-distance weights, add the Euclidean barycentre identity, and
then take the supremum in $p$.  This observation is the bridge between
the scalar exact-star smoothing and the mixed Hessian required here.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Finite activity and finite dual sampling.}
Choose nested finite sets $K_n\subset K$ with union $K$, stopping if
$K$ is finite.  Define scalar profiles, for every $p$, by
\begin{align}
 h_{n,a}(t,p)&=\max\{f_a(t,p),f_0(p)-n\}, &&a\in A,
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-truncate-a}\\
 h_{n,b}(t,p)&=\max\{f_b(t,p),f_0(p)-n\}, &&b\in K_n,
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-truncate-k}\\
 h_{n,b}(t,p)&=f_0(p), &&b\in B\setminus(A\cup K_n).
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-truncate-rest}
\end{align}
The slope-budget and truncation argument in the exact-star theorem shows
that each $h_n(\,cdot\,,p)$ is a finite continuous, finite-active member
of $\mathscr J_B(D)$.  It also gives
\begin{equation}
 h_{n+1}(x,p)\leq h_n(x,p),
 \qquad h_n(x,p)\longrightarrow f_x(p).
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-profile-limit}
\end{equation}
On a newly retained branch, the first inequality uses
$f_b(t,p)\leq f_0(p)$, the monotonicity of a full scalar comparison
profile towards the node.

Let $H_n$ be reconstructed from $h_n$ by
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-reconstruction}.  Local convex
biconjugacy on $\operatorname{int}Q$ gives the explicit formula
\begin{equation}
 H_{n,b}(t,y)=
 \begin{cases}
  \max\{u_b(t,y),c(y)-n\},&b\in A\cup K_n,\\
  c(y),&b\in B\setminus(A\cup K_n).
 \end{cases}
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-truncated-reconstruction}
\end{equation}
The formula remains valid at a full endpoint: if the endpoint slice is
finite, use its supporting covectors; if it is identically $-\infty$,
only the second entry of the maximum remains.  Hence
\begin{equation}
 H_{n+1}\leq H_n,
 \qquad H_n\longrightarrow u
 \quad\text{pointwise on }D\times V.
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-H-limit}
\end{equation}

Each $H_n$ is finite and continuous on
$D\times\overline V$.  On finite branch strata this follows from finite
joint convexity.  We record why pointwise continuity in the branch
variable is enough at the node.  If a finite convex function $q$ on
$[-R,0]\times V_0$ has continuous boundary value
$q(0,y)=c_q(y)$ and
$q(t,y)\to c_q(y)$ for every fixed $y$, then $q$ is continuous at
every point of $\{0\}\times V_0$.  For the upper bound, write a nearby
$(t,y)$ as a convex combination of $(0,z)$ and $(-R,w)$, with
$w$ fixed and the coefficient of $(-R,w)$ tending to zero.  For the
lower bound, first choose $t_0<0$ so that
$q(t_0,y_0)$ is close to $c_q(y_0)$, then write
$(t_0,y_0)$ as a convex combination of the nearby $(t,y)$ and a point
$(-R,z)$.  Solving the convexity inequality for $q(t,y)$, and using
boundedness of the finite convex slice $q(-R,\,\cdot\,)$ on a compact
Euclidean neighbourhood, gives the lower bound.  This proves the claim.

Only finitely many branches of $H_n$ are active.  Apply the boundary lemma
to each of them.  The scalar endpoint-slope bounds give its fixed-$y$
hypothesis, while every inactive branch is exactly $c(y)$.  The
cofinite-branch topology now gives continuity at the node.

At a full endpoint, choose any sequence of branch parameters decreasing to
$-\infty$.  Equations
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-endpoint-trace} and
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-truncated-reconstruction} give monotone
convergence of the corresponding continuous Euclidean slices to the finite
convex endpoint slice.  Dini's theorem makes this convergence uniform on
$\overline V$; branch monotonicity then makes the estimate uniform for all
sufficiently terminal parameters.  Since $D$ is compact, so is
$D\times\overline V$.

Fix a summable positive sequence $(\varepsilon_n)$.  For each point of
that compact product, choose a covector which realizes
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-reconstruction} within
$\varepsilon_n$.  Continuity of the corresponding scalar profile on
$D$ supplies a neighbourhood on which the same choice works.  A finite
subcover gives covectors $p_{n,1},\ldots,p_{n,q_n}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 H_n-\varepsilon_n\leq
 A_n:=\max_j\bigl(p_{n,j}\mathbin\cdot y
                 +h_n(x,p_{n,j})\bigr)
 \leq H_n
 \quad\text{on }D\times\overline V.
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-finite-dual-sampling}
\end{equation}
No compactness of the full dual space is used.

For each selected profile, truncation is inactive on a sufficiently short
node collar.  Its endpoint derivatives are therefore the finite derivatives
of the corresponding scalar comparison profile, and their sum is
nonpositive by the scalar slope balance.  Choose once a smaller standard
neighbourhood $U'$ with closure in $D$.  The finite harmonic smoothing
from the exact-star theorem then gives, for every selected covector, a smooth
psh scalar function $s_{n,j}$ on that same $U'$ with
\[
 \bigl\lVert s_{n,j}-h_n(\,cdot\,,p_{n,j})\bigr\rVert_{U'}
 <\varepsilon_n.
\]
Thus $s_{n,j}+2\varepsilon_n$ lies between the scalar profile plus
$\varepsilon_n$ and that profile plus $3\varepsilon_n$.  The lifted
function
\[
 (x,y)\longmapsto
 s_{n,j}(x)+2\varepsilon_n+p_{n,j}\mathbin\cdot y
\]
is an exact product generator.  Apply a smooth convex coordinatewise
nondecreasing regularized maximum to these finitely many lifts, with error
at most $\varepsilon_n$, and add one further $\varepsilon_n$.  The
result is a generator $W_n$ on $U'\times V$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
                         H_n\leq W_n\leq H_n+5\varepsilon_n.
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-smoothing-error}
\end{equation}
The balance law survives the regularized maximum.  At the node, its partial
derivatives with respect to the finitely many inputs are independent of the
branch, so summing first over the branches reduces
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-smooth-balance} to the corresponding
balance for each input.  A finite union of activity sets is finite, and a
common terminal collar exists for every full active branch.  Joint
convexity follows from convex monotone composition.

Set
\[
 d_n=5\sum_{k>n}\varepsilon_k,
 \qquad G_n=W_n+d_n.
\]
Equations \eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-H-limit} and
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-smoothing-error} give
\[
 G_{n+1}\leq H_{n+1}+5\varepsilon_{n+1}+d_{n+1}
 \leq H_n+d_n\leq G_n.
\]
Moreover, $G_n\to u$ pointwise.  This proves the fixed-neighbourhood
first-stage approximation at every finite node value.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{The value $-\infty$, full endpoints, and interior points.}
If $c(y_0)=-\infty$, joint convexity makes $c$ identically
$-\infty$ after a Euclidean shrinking.  On every full branch, the scalar
exact trace and convexity then force the whole branch to be
$-\infty$; on the finitely many exceptional collars, joint convexity
forces $-\infty$ after one common shrinking.  Thus the germ is
identically $-\infty$, and the constants $-n$ give the required
approximation.

It remains to treat a point $(-\infty,y_0)$ in a full branch.  Work on
$[ -\infty,R)\times V_0$, where $R<0$.  The identically $-\infty$
case is again immediate.  Otherwise the function is finite on the finite
stratum and is nondecreasing in the branch variable.  Choose $r<R_1<R$,
an open convex set $V\ni y_0$, and a compact convex set $Q$ with
$\overline V\subset\operatorname{int}Q\Subset V_0$, and put
\begin{align*}
 f(t,p)&=\min_{y\in Q}\bigl(u(t,y)-p\mathbin\cdot y\bigr),\\
 f_1(p)&=\min_{y\in Q}\bigl(u(R_1,y)-p\mathbin\cdot y\bigr),\\
 h_n(t,p)&=\max\{f(t,p),f_1(p)-n\}.
\end{align*}
Then $h_n(\,cdot\,,p)$ is finite, convex, nondecreasing, and has the
exact endpoint trace.  Its reconstruction is
\begin{equation}
 H_n(t,y)=\max\{u(t,y),u(R_1,y)-n\},
 \label{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-endpoint-truncation}
\end{equation}
so $H_n\downarrow u$ and every $H_n$ is continuous on the compact
terminal core $[ -\infty,r]\times\overline V$.  The endpoint continuity
again follows from Dini's theorem.

Fix a summable positive sequence $(\varepsilon_n)$.  Finite dual sampling
on the compact terminal core gives covectors
$p_{n,1},\ldots,p_{n,q_n}$ such that
\[
 H_n-\varepsilon_n\leq
 A_n:=\max_j\bigl(p_{n,j}\mathbin\cdot y
                 +h_n(t,p_{n,j})\bigr)\leq H_n.
\]
For each selected scalar profile, use the endpoint construction in the
proof of \Cref{thm:p071-infinite-star-collapse-candidate}.  It supplies a
decreasing sequence of smooth convex functions, constant on terminal
collars, with limit $h_n$.  Since $h_n$ is finite and continuous on the
compact endpoint interval, Dini's theorem permits the choice of one term
$s_{n,j}$ satisfying
\[
       h_n(\,cdot\,,p_{n,j})\leq s_{n,j}\leq
       h_n(\,cdot\,,p_{n,j})+\varepsilon_n.
\]
Add $2\varepsilon_n$ to the finitely many lifted functions
$s_{n,j}(t)+p_{n,j}\mathbin\cdot y$, apply the same regularized maximum
with error at most $\varepsilon_n$, and add one further
$\varepsilon_n$.  The resulting exact product generator $W_n$ satisfies
\[
                       H_n\leq W_n\leq H_n+5\varepsilon_n
\]
on one fixed terminal product neighbourhood.  The neighbourhood is
independent of $n$; only finitely many selected profiles occur at each
stage, so their constant collars have a common terminal subcollar.  Set
\[
 d_n=5\sum_{k>n}\varepsilon_k,\qquad G_n=W_n+d_n.
\]
Since $H_{n+1}\leq H_n$, the same calculation as at the node gives
\[
 G_{n+1}\leq H_{n+1}+5\varepsilon_{n+1}+d_{n+1}
 \leq H_n+d_n\leq G_n.
\]
Moreover $G_n\to u$ pointwise.  Thus the $G_n$ give the required
decreasing exact product generators on one fixed terminal neighbourhood.

At an interior branch point, a locally extended-real jointly convex
function is either identically $-\infty$ or finite.  In the finite case,
the point lies in an ordinary open convex chart in
$\mathbf R^{d+1}$.  The one-point Stone case of
\Cref{thm:p071-stone-euclidean-collapse} therefore gives a decreasing
smooth jointly convex approximation on one fixed smaller chart.  We have
therefore proved
$\mathcal J_X\subseteq\mathcal P_{X,1}$ at every point.  Together with
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-minimality} and the tautological inclusion
$\mathcal P_{X,1}\subseteq\mathcal P_X$, this proves
\eqref{eq:p071-infinite-euclidean-collapse} and the fixed-neighbourhood
assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Write $\mathcal J_{\mathrm{eucl}}$ and
$\mathcal G_{\mathrm{eucl},0}$ for the exact comparison and generator
sheaves of
\Cref{thm:p071-infinite-star-euclidean-collapse} with one Euclidean
coordinate.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Locality and decreasing closure.}
All displayed comparison conditions are local.  The contraction argument
in the proof of the cited theorem shows that the junction inequality is
unchanged when a full branch becomes exceptional after a restriction; the
same argument works at $s=0$ because the homothety in the $s$-coordinate
preserves the half-interval.  Joint convexity glues on branch products, the
full-endpoint trace glues on a terminal branch collar, and the
boundary-minimum condition glues on the connected endpoint component.
Thus $\mathcal J_+$ is a sheaf.

It is closed under pointwise decreasing sequential limits.  Joint
extended-real convexity, the boundary-minimum inequality, and the junction
inequality pass to the limit exactly as in the Euclidean product theorem.
For the latter, if the limiting central value is finite, all finitely many
values in the displayed tuple are finite, so ordinary termwise passage is
legitimate.  The full-endpoint trace passes by the monotonicity argument in
that theorem.  At a node, compactness of a closed endpoint interval and the
cofinite-branch topology give one countable activity set for each row; the
union of those sets over the sequence is still countable and works for the
limit.

Every generator belongs to $\mathcal J_+$.  On the finite stratum this is
the generator inclusion of the Euclidean product theorem.  On its initial
constant collar, the boundary minimum is immediate.  Beyond that collar,
joint convexity makes the generator nondecreasing in $s$, because its
$s$-derivative starts at zero and is nondecreasing along every vertical
line.  The same derivative-balance calculation as in the cited theorem
gives \eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-jensen}, now allowing some or all
of the $s$-coordinates to be zero.  Minimality therefore gives
\begin{equation}
                         \mathcal P_+\subseteq\mathcal J_+.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-minimality}
\end{equation}

\medskip\noindent
\emph{A monotone-coordinate refinement of the Euclidean theorem.}
We record the exact refinement needed below.  If
$v\in\mathcal J_{\mathrm{eucl}}$ is nondecreasing in its Euclidean
coordinate, then the fixed-neighbourhood approximating sequence supplied
by \Cref{thm:p071-infinite-star-euclidean-collapse} may be chosen as
\begin{equation}
             g_{n+1}\leq g_n,\qquad g_n\downarrow v,
             \qquad \partial_s g_n\geq0.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-monotone-refinement}
\end{equation}

Here are the details, including the extended-real star endpoints.  In the
partial-Legendre step of the proof of the Euclidean theorem, work on the
same compact inner interval in the $s$-variable.  A finite convex function
which is nondecreasing in $s$ is the supremum, on every smaller interval,
of its supporting affine functions whose $s$-slopes are nonnegative.
Accordingly, every finite dual sample in that proof may be chosen with
nonnegative $s$-component.  The scalar exact-star truncations and scalar
star smoothing do not alter that component.  Each lifted smooth function
therefore has nonnegative $s$-derivative, and a smooth convex
coordinatewise nondecreasing regularized maximum preserves this property.

At a full star endpoint, the proof first replaces $v$ by
\[
                 H_m(x,s)=\max\{v(x,s),v(x_1,s)-m\}
\]
on a compact terminal core, for one fixed finite branch point $x_1$.
Both entries are nondecreasing in $s$, so $H_m$ is also nondecreasing.
The same nonnegative-slope dual sampling and endpoint smoothing therefore
apply.  If a node central value is $-\infty$, the cited proof uses constant
approximants after shrinking, which already have zero $s$-derivative.  At
an ordinary branch point, extend a finite jointly convex nondecreasing
function to a slightly larger convex set as a supremum of supporting
affine functions with nonnegative $s$-slope, take a finite maximum on the
chosen compact core, and mollify; this gives the same property.  Finally,
the summable tail constants used to impose exact decrease do not change any
derivative.  These observations prove
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-monotone-refinement} in every stratum.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Convex extension across the finite collar endpoint.}
Let $u\in\mathcal J_+$ near a point $(x_0,0)$.  Shrink to a displayed
product neighbourhood $V_X\times[0,r)$.  For each fixed $x$, joint
convexity and
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-boundary-minimum} show that
$s\mapsto u(x,s)$ is nondecreasing.  Define on
$V_X\times(-r,r)$
\begin{equation}
             \widetilde u(x,s)=u\bigl(x,s^+\bigr),
             \qquad s^+=\max\{s,0\}.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-extension}
\end{equation}
We claim that $\widetilde u\in\mathcal J_{\mathrm{eucl}}$ after one
harmless shrinking.

On each ordinary branch product, this follows from the standard convex
composition rule: the inner map fixes the branch coordinate and replaces
$s$ by the convex function $s^+$, while the outer jointly convex function
is nondecreasing in its second variable.  The exact full-branch endpoint
trace and the common countable activity condition pass unchanged through
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-extension}.

It remains to check the product junction inequality.  Take a junction
tuple for $\widetilde u$ with central coordinate $s_0$ and branch
coordinates $s_i$, using reciprocal-distance weights whose sum is
$\Lambda$.  Put
\[
             q=\Lambda^{-1}\sum_i\lambda_i s_i^+,
             \qquad \lambda_i\in
               \{1/r_b:b\in F\}\cup\{1/\rho_a:a\in A\}.
\]
The original barycentre relation gives
\begin{equation}
                         q\geq s_0^+.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-positive-part-barycentre}
\end{equation}
After shrinking the ambient interval once, $q$ remains in $[0,r)$.
Since $c$ is nondecreasing, the junction inequality for $u$, applied at
the centre coordinate $q$ and the sample coordinates $s_i^+$, gives
\[
 \Lambda\widetilde c(s_0)
   =\Lambda c(s_0^+)
   \leq\Lambda c(q)
   \leq\sum_i\lambda_i u_i(s_i^+)
   =\sum_i\lambda_i\widetilde u_i(s_i).
\]
This is precisely the required junction inequality for the extension.
The claim follows.

Apply the monotone-coordinate refinement to obtain, on one fixed smaller
product neighbourhood $V_X'\times(-\delta,r')$,
\begin{equation}
        g_{n+1}\leq g_n,qquad g_n\downarrow\widetilde u,
        \qquad \partial_sg_n\geq0,
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-euclidean-approximants}
\end{equation}
with $g_n\in\mathcal G_{\mathrm{eucl},0}$.

\medskip\noindent
\emph{Restoring exact constant collars.}
Choose a smooth convex nondecreasing function
$\phi:[0,+\infty)\to\mathbf R$ which is constant near zero, agrees with
the identity for $q\geq2$, and satisfies $\phi(q)\geq q$.  Such a function
is obtained by choosing a smooth nondecreasing derivative which is zero
near zero and one on $[2,+\infty)$, and then choosing the integration
constant so that $\phi(2)=2$.  For $a>0$, put
\begin{equation}
                         h_a(s)=a\phi(s/a).
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-clamp}
\end{equation}
Then $h_a$ is smooth, convex, nondecreasing, constant on an initial
interval, and equal to $s$ for $s\geq2a$.  Moreover
\begin{equation}
              0<a'<a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h_{a'}\leq h_a.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-clamp-order}
\end{equation}
Indeed, with $q=s/a$,
\[
       \frac{\partial}{\partial a}\bigl(a\phi(s/a)\bigr)
          =\phi(q)-q\phi'(q)\geq0;
\]
the last function is nonincreasing in $q$ and equals zero for $q\geq2$.

After shrinking $V_X'$ once more, choose a compact closed standard star
core $D$ contained in the fixed domain of the $g_n$ and containing the
closure of $V_X'$ in its interior.  Fix $0<r''<r'$.  Recursively
choose $a_n\downarrow0$ so rapidly that $a_{n+1}<a_n/2$, the image of
$[0,r'')$ under $h_{a_n}$ lies in $(-\delta,r')$, and
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{(x,s)\in D\times[0,r'']}
    \bigl|g_n(x,h_{a_n}(s))-g_n(x,s)\bigr|<\frac1n.
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-uniform-clamp-error}
\end{equation}
This is possible because each real-valued generator $g_n$ is uniformly
continuous on a slightly larger compact core and $h_a\to\operatorname{id}$
uniformly on compact half-intervals.

Set
\begin{equation}
                     G_n(x,s)=g_n(x,h_{a_n}(s)).
\label{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-final-approximants}
\end{equation}
The function $G_n$ is an exact product generator.  Joint convexity follows
from convex monotone composition.  It is independent of $s$ on an initial
collar.  At the star node, its finite activity set is that of $g_n$ and
\[
 \sum_b\partial_tG_{n,b}(0,s)
   =\sum_b\partial_tg_{n,b}(0,h_{a_n}(s))=0.
\]
The terminal-collar property at a full star endpoint is also unchanged.

Equations
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-monotone-refinement} and
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-clamp-order} give
\[
 G_{n+1}(x,s)
 =g_{n+1}(x,h_{a_{n+1}}(s))
 \leq g_n(x,h_{a_{n+1}}(s))
 \leq g_n(x,h_{a_n}(s))=G_n(x,s).
\]
By \eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-uniform-clamp-error} and
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-euclidean-approximants},
$G_n(x,s)\to u(x,s)$ pointwise on
$V_X'\times[0,r'')$, including every extended-real value on a full star
endpoint.  Thus every endpoint germ in $\mathcal J_+$ belongs to
$\mathcal P_{+,1}$ on one fixed smaller product neighbourhood.

At a point with positive $S_+$-coordinate, the assertion is exactly
\Cref{thm:p071-infinite-star-euclidean-collapse}.  Hence
$\mathcal J_+\subseteq\mathcal P_{+,1}$ everywhere.  Together with
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-minimality} and the tautological
inclusion $\mathcal P_{+,1}\subseteq\mathcal P_+$, this proves
\eqref{eq:p071-star-finite-collar-collapse} and the fixed-neighbourhood
assertion.
\end{proof}
